blocks.text: 1-year prevalence of depression in the general population is 5.3%; lifetime prevalence 13%. **NESARC**: mean age of onset 30 years; first episode occurs before age 40 in ~50% of patients.
Most common comorbidities: alcohol use (>40%) and anxiety (>40%); 30% have a personality disorder. Suicide is attempted by 9% of those with **MDD**.

In ~56% of patients the initial diagnosis of depressive disorder changes on follow-up — mainly to schizophrenic spectrum (16%), personality disorder (9%), neurotic/stress-related/somatoform (8%), or bipolar disorder (8%) (Kessing, 2005).

blocks.title: The 5 Rs of depression course
rows: No meaningful symptoms on scales (e.g. **HAMD**<7), sustained past the natural episode length (usually >3 months)
Sustained past the natural untreated-episode length (usually >6 months)
Repeat symptoms before the recovery threshold is reached (i.e. during remission)
Repeat symptoms after the recovery threshold is reached

blocks.text: Untreated depressive episode lasts 6–13 months; most treated episodes last ~3 months. Probability of recurrence rises with episode count: ~50% recurrence within 5 years after one episode, ~70% after two episodes, 80–95% after three.
Major depression carries up to a 5-fold increased risk of **MI**; suicide among mood-disorder patients overall is ~14x more frequent than in the general population.

Treat comorbid depression before anxiety if both are present. Watchful waiting (review in 2 weeks) for mild depression if agreeable; antidepressants are not advocated for mild depression given a poor risk–benefit ratio there.
"Which comorbidity should be treated first?" → **NICE** explicitly wants comorbid depression treated **BEFORE** anxiety — treating anxiety first is presented as the wrong (non-recommended) answer.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: SSRIs are first-line antidepressants. For severe depression at presentation, combine antidepressant + **CBT** (more cost-effective than either alone). Continue antidepressants ≥6 months after remission for a moderate/severe episode; ≥2 years if >2 recent episodes or residual impairment.

**ECT** is reserved for rapid/short-term improvement of severe symptoms after an adequate trial of other treatment has failed, and/or when the condition is potentially life-threatening; **ECT** maintenance is not recommended.

Antidepressant response/remission NNTs (**FDA** reanalysis): adults **NNT** ~4–5 for response, ~6–7 for remission over 12–14-week trials. In the elderly, **NNT** is 4 for tricyclics, 8 for SSRIs, 3 for MAOIs.

Kirsch's meta-analysis (47 **FDA** trials): drug–placebo **HRSD** difference was only 1.80 points overall, below **NICE**'s 3-point clinical-significance threshold — but the effect size grew with baseline severity, exceeding the **NICE**-significant threshold only above an **HRSD** baseline of ~28.

Antidepressants and suicide: **MHRA**/**FDA** black-box warning applies to under-25s (risk neutral 25–64, protective ≥65). **BAP** (2015): **SSRI** treatment is not associated with increased completed suicide in adults and is linked to a small (<1%) rise in non-fatal suicidal ideation in adolescents/young adults.

"Do antidepressants increase suicide risk?" — the expected, guideline-backed answer is that suicides occur **MORE** often among those **NOT** on an antidepressant; don't let the black-box-warning framing pull you toward the intuitive-but-wrong answer.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Antidepressant toxicity in overdose (Hawton 2010): TCAs > **venlafaxine**/**mirtazapine** > SSRIs in toxicity. Within TCAs, **dosulepin** and **doxepin** are more toxic than **amitriptyline**; within SSRIs, **citalopram** has the highest case fatality.
The 5 A's behind apparent (pseudo-)treatment resistance: Alcoholism, lack of Adequate dosage, lack of Adherence, Axis 2 disorders, Alternate diagnoses (e.g. **PTSD**).

blocks.forTopic: Causes of apparent (pseudo-) treatment resistance in depression

blocks.text: **STAR*D** (pragmatic **RCT**, n=4041): Level 1 **citalopram**; Level 2 switch (**bupropion** SR/**sertraline**/**venlafaxine** XR) or augment (**bupropion**/**buspirone**) or combine with **CBT**; Level 3 switch to **mirtazapine**/**nortriptyline** or augment with **lithium**/thyroid hormone; Level 4 switch to **tranylcypromine** (**MAOI**) or **venlafaxine**+**mirtazapine** combo. Remission fell and relapse rose at each successive level (37%→31%→14%→13% remission). Cumulative remission after all 4 steps: 67%.

blocks.forTopic: STAR*D step order for treatment-resistant depression
blocks.mnemonic: "CITalopram, SWITCH or Add, MIRtazapine or Nortriptyline, then MAOI" — C-S-M-M
expansion: Level 2: Switch (**bupropion**/**sertraline**/**venlafaxine**) or augment (**bupropion**/**buspirone**) or combine with **CBT**
Level 3: switch to **Mirtazapine**/**nortriptyline**, or augment with **lithium**/**T3**
Level 4: switch to a **MAOI** (**tranylcypromine**) or combine **venlafaxine**+**mirtazapine**

blocks.title: STAR*D — remission and relapse by treatment level
columns: Level 3 (switch to mirtazapine/nortriptyline or augment Li/T3)
Level 4 (switch to MAOI or VFX/MZP combo)

blocks.text: Combining two antidepressants: evidence base is sparse. **Venlafaxine** + **mirtazapine** ("Californian rocket fuel") has some support in **TRD**. Serotonin syndrome is a particular risk with **SSRI**+**MAOI** combinations. No single combination has proven superior head-to-head.

**NCS-R** lifetime prevalence: bipolar I 1.0%, bipolar **II** 1.1%, subsyndromal bipolar spectrum 2.4%. Mean age of onset: **BP-I** 18.2 years, **BP-II** ~20 years. Suicide rate in bipolar disorder is 15–18x the general population.

Once diagnosed, bipolar disorder's diagnostic stability is 70–91%; bipolar I is more stable than bipolar **II** (**II** can switch to I but not vice versa). **NICE**: recurrence risk after a mood episode is ~50% at 1 year and >70% at 4 years.

blocks.title: Unipolar vs Bipolar Depression — Differentiating Features

blocks.text: Bipolar **II** patients spend more time depressed than bipolar I (93% vs 67% of symptomatic time is depressive) — thought to explain higher suicidality/poorer functional recovery in bipolar **II** despite "milder" mania.
Perlis (**STEP-BD**): the single biggest predictor of relapse is residual symptoms, and most relapses are into depression.

Rapid cycling = ≥4 episodes/year; ultra-rapid = ≥4/month; ultradian = switching within a day on ≥4 days/week. ~20% of bipolar patients rapid-cycle (**STEP-BD**); ~80% of rapid cyclers are women. Current hypothyroidism and poor **lithium** response are associated with rapid cycling.

"Switch" (antidepressant-induced mania, within ~2 months of starting) is distinct from "mood destabilization" (long-term increase in episode frequency from antidepressant use) — a drug can cause one without the other.

Acute de novo mania: antipsychotic first-line (**haloperidol**, **olanzapine**, **quetiapine** or **risperidone**) for rapid anti-manic effect. Do **NOT** offer **lamotrigine** for mania. If already on an antidepressant, consider stopping it, then offer an antipsychotic regardless.

Bipolar depression: offer a bipolar-specific/high-intensity psychological intervention first-line. If drug-naive with moderate/severe bipolar depression, **NICE** suggests **fluoxetine**+**olanzapine** combination, or **quetiapine** alone. Second step: **lamotrigine**.

Maintenance: **lithium** monotherapy first-line — more effective against mania than depression, and reduces suicide risk. **Valproate** probably prevents both manic and depressive relapse; **olanzapine** prevents manic more than depressive relapse; **lamotrigine** prevents depressive more than manic relapse; **carbamazepine** is less effective than **lithium**.
**Lithium** toxicity with neurological symptoms → haemodialysis is the expected answer once levels exceed the life-threatening 2.0 mmol/L threshold, not simply stopping the drug.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **NICE** maintenance duration: continue ≥2 years after an episode, up to 5 years if high relapse-risk factors are present.
Mixed episodes: treat as manic episodes, avoid antidepressants; best evidence is for **valproate** (more effective than **lithium**/placebo).

Bauer's definition: a true "mood stabiliser" must show efficacy in all four of acute mania, acute depression, manic prophylaxis, and depressive prophylaxis — by that strict definition, only **lithium** qualifies.
Incidence 7–42 per 100,000 depending on criteria (**WHO** 7-country study). Male:female incidence ratio ~1.4:1. Migrants have 3–5x the incidence of the native population.
Median prevalence: 4.6/1000 point, 3.3/1000 period, 4.0/1000 lifetime (not 1% as **DSM** often states), 7.2/1000 lifetime morbid risk (Saha 2004). No significant sex difference in prevalence.
Genetic risk rises with relatedness: ~12–15% if one first-degree relative affected, 40–50% if both parents affected.
Cannabis: pooled **OR** for later psychosis ~2.1 (95% **CI** 1.7–2.5); dose-response relationship; exposure by age 15 confers a higher (fourfold) risk than later exposure.
**AESOP** study: all psychoses are more common in Black and minority ethnic groups vs White population in the **UK** (crude **IRR** 3.6, adjusted **IRR** 2.9 after age/sex/site).

items.text: Risk of schizophrenia if **BOTH** parents affected is 40–50% — don't confuse with the single first-degree-relative figure of 12–15%; both numbers are tested.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: Cannabis by age 15 confers a fourfold (not the general twofold) increased schizophrenia risk — the exam distinguishes the age-15 figure from the overall-adolescent figure.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: Positive family history of schizophrenia is a **GENETIC** factor, not an environmental one — a classification trap in "which is **NOT** an environmental risk factor" questions.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: **ICD-11** removed schizophrenia's **ICD-10** descriptive subtypes (paranoid, hebephrenic, etc.) specifically because of their lack of prognostic validity and treatment utility — a favoured "why was this changed" trap.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Clozapine** is the only drug showing moderate-to-large effect-size superiority over FGAs (in resistant illness, not first-episode). **CATIE** and **CUtLASS** found SGAs no better than FGAs on efficacy/cost overall.

No **RCT** evidence for a first-generation "correct" mean dose, but there is for SGAs. Near-maximal effective doses: **haloperidol** 3.3–10mg/day; **aripiprazole** 10mg/day; **olanzapine** possibly >16mg/day; **risperidone** 4mg/day (2mg gives lower efficacy; ≥10mg no added benefit, more **EPSE**).

blocks.title: Approximate near-maximal-efficacy antipsychotic doses
rows: possibly >16mg/day; 5mg/day quoted as a comparator dose

blocks.text: **NICE** for a first episode: oral atypical first-line; **clozapine** at the earliest sign of treatment resistance; do not routinely switch a well-controlled patient on a typical to an atypical; atypicals and typicals should not be co-prescribed except briefly during a changeover.
Maintenance: ~20% relapse within a year on treatment vs ~60% off it; stopping medication raises relapse risk ~5-fold. Multi-episode patients: maintenance for ≥5 years, possibly indefinite.

Depot myths (Maudsley): **NMS** risk is not higher for depot vs oral; **NMS** history is not a depot contraindication; tardive dyskinesia risk is not higher for depot vs oral of the same drug; many patients on depot prefer it once tried.

blocks.title: Depot antipsychotic notable profiles (Maudsley)
rows: More effective in aggression; higher **EPSE** burden
Useful for manic relapse prevention; needs 3–6 months to steady state
Needs fridge storage; no test dose required

blocks.text: Royal College high-dose prescribing (>1g **chlorpromazine**-equivalent): avoid wherever possible; no evidence it helps non-responders; **ECG** before and periodically during; increase dose no more than weekly; stop after 3 months if no response.

items.text: "Which depot has higher **EPSE** burden but favourable symptom control?" → **Zuclopenthixol**. A classic depot-profile recall question, not clinical reasoning.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: Depot myths trap: tardive dyskinesia risk is **NOT** higher for depot vs oral formulations of the same drug, and **NMS** history is **NOT** a contraindication to depot use — the exam expects you to know these are myths, not intuit them.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: Weight gain + hyperglycaemia on an antipsychotic → the expected answer is **olanzapine** (strongest evidence for both, alongside **clozapine**) — don't default to **clozapine** here since the vignette isn't about treatment resistance.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: "Except" question on **NICE** schizophrenia guidance: combined antipsychotic prescriptions are **NOT** endorsed even in first-episode illness — the exam expects you to reject combination therapy as a **NICE**-endorsed practice in any context except brief medication changeover.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **NICE** treatment-resistance definition: lack of satisfactory response to sequential adequate (6–8 week) trials of ≥2 antipsychotics, at least one being a non-**clozapine** atypical.

Kane et al. (1988): **clozapine** 30% responders vs **chlorpromazine** 4% in treatment-resistant illness. Meltzer: ~30% respond by 6 weeks, a further 20% by 3 months, 10–20% more by 6 months — trial **clozapine** monotherapy for at least 6 months. Plasma level ~350–450 ng/mL is the usual non-response threshold.
Best evidence for suicide-risk reduction in schizophrenia is **clozapine** (**InterSePT** trial vs **olanzapine**) — a very frequently tested factual pairing.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **CATIE**: pragmatic **RCT**, 1493 patients, **olanzapine**/**quetiapine**/**risperidone**/**ziprasidone**/**perphenazine**. 74% discontinued within 18 months overall; **olanzapine** had the lowest discontinuation (64%) but highest metabolic side-effect burden. In the **clozapine**-vs-other-**SGA** phase, **clozapine** had the lowest discontinuation, ~3x longer time-to-discontinuation.
**CATIE**'s first-generation comparator drug was **perphenazine** specifically (not **haloperidol**) — a commonly misremembered detail.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **CUtLASS**: unblinded **RCT**, no advantage of SGAs over FGAs for quality of life/symptoms at 1 year (**FGA** group did relatively better). **CUtLASS** 2: **clozapine** showed significant symptom advantage over other SGAs in non-responders, and patients preferred it.

blocks.title: Good Prognostic Factors
rows: Family history of affective (not schizophrenic) disorder

blocks.title: Relapse within 1 year — antipsychotics vs placebo

blocks.text: High expressed emotion (Brown & Rutter) raises relapse risk despite adequate pharmacotherapy; family therapy cuts relapse from ~64% to ~24% in such families (Cochrane **NNT** ~6, Pharaoh 2000).

Long-term outcome studies (Iowa 500, Bonn, Chestnut Lodge, Vermont, **WHO** ISoS/DOSMeD) consistently show a more favourable long-term course than clinicians typically assume, and better outcomes in developing countries than developed ones.
Point prevalence 1–3% (adults); lifetime ~2–3%.

blocks.title: Four-factor symptom model of OCD (Castle & Phillips)

blocks.text: Symmetry and hoarding subtypes tend to be more chronic/treatment-resistant than the other two factors.

**PANDAS** diagnostic criteria: **OCD** or tic disorder; onset age 3–puberty; abrupt onset/dramatic exacerbations; symptom exacerbation temporally linked to group-A strep infection; abnormal neuro exam (hyperactivity, choreiform movements/tics) during exacerbation.

**NICE** stepped care: mild–moderate → self-help → **CBT** with exposure and response prevention (**ERP**) → **SSRI** ± **CBT**. Severe → **SSRI** ± **CBT** first. Continue a responding **SSRI** 1–2 years ± booster **CBT**. **SSRI** doses needed are higher than for depression; **NNT** vs placebo is 6–12.

**NCS-R** lifetime prevalence 6.8% (men 3.6%, women 9.7%) despite men being more often exposed to trauma overall — women develop **PTSD** roughly twice as often even after controlling for trauma type. Rape is the one trauma type where men develop more **PTSD** than women.

**NICE**: watchful waiting if symptoms mild and <4 weeks post-trauma. Trauma-focused **CBT** or **EMDR** for symptoms present >3 months (up to 12 sessions); **paroxetine**/**mirtazapine** general use, **amitriptyline**/**phenelzine** specialist use — **paroxetine** and **sertraline** are the only SSRIs licensed for **PTSD** in the **UK** (**sertraline** licensed for females only).

**EMI** on **PTSD** timing: watchful waiting (<4 weeks post-trauma) vs trauma-focused **CBT** (within 3 months) vs **EMDR** (>3 months, or after **CBT** failure) — the exam tests the exact time cut-offs, not just "offer therapy".

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/EMIs Adult Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Acute stress reaction: immediate, clear temporal link to an exceptional stressor; symptoms usually resolve within 2–3 days (often hours); a mixed, changing symptom picture (numbness, depression, anxiety, anger, overactivity, withdrawal) rather than one dominant symptom.

**GAD** lifetime prevalence ~5%; **NICE** first-line is an **SSRI** (**SNRI**/**pregabalin** alternatives); insufficient evidence to recommend combined drug+psychological treatment as an initial strategy.

Panic disorder point prevalence 0.9%; mean onset age ~22. **NICE**: 7–14 hours of **CBT** over ≤4 months, or **SSRI** first-line; switch to **imipramine**/**clomipramine** if no improvement after 12 weeks of **SSRI**. Benzodiazepines are associated with worse long-term outcome and should not be prescribed.

Social phobia point prevalence 2.8%. **CBT** and SSRIs are best-established; benzodiazepines should not be used. **Phenelzine** is second-line; beta-blockers are not better than placebo for the generalised subtype but can help the performance-only subtype.
**Kava** (Piper methysticum) has trial evidence for anxiolysis but is withdrawn from the **UK** market due to hepatotoxicity risk — cannot be recommended clinically despite the evidence base.
**DSM-5** dropped the amenorrhoea criterion for anorexia — amenorrhoeic and menstruating patients with the same **BMI**/body-image disturbance have similar clinical features and outcome.
Heritability: anorexia nervosa **MZ** 55% vs **DZ** 5% (significant heritable component); bulimia nervosa **MZ** 35% vs **DZ** 30% (heritability not significant).

Bradycardia (**HR** ~40 common), orthostatic hypotension and **QT** prolongation are the classic cardiac findings in anorexia; hypercarotenaemia, lanugo hair, Russell's sign (knuckle calluses from induced vomiting) and perimylolysis (dental erosion) are classic physical signs.

Bulimia is **NOT** associated with peptic ulcer — oesophageal tears, dental erosion, seizures (electrolyte-related) and parotid enlargement are the tested complications; peptic ulcer is the deliberate distractor.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **NICE**: drugs must not be sole/primary treatment for anorexia. For bulimia, evidence-based self-help is first-line; **fluoxetine** is first-choice drug at a higher-than-antidepressant dose (60mg/day); **CBT** 16–20 sessions over 4–5 months.

5–13% of the general population has ≥1 personality disorder; borderline **PD** is generally the most prevalent in psychiatric settings; antisocial (dissocial) **PD** is the most prevalent category in prison settings (63% of male remand prisoners in a England & Wales survey).

blocks.title: Personality disorder cluster prevalence (Coid 2006, GB community sample, weighted per 1000)

blocks.mnemonic: Cluster A = Weird, Cluster B = Wild, Cluster C = Worried
expansion: Cluster B (antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic) — dramatic/erratic

blocks.text: Borderline **PD**: ~2% general population, 10% outpatients, 15–20% inpatients; female:male ratio ~3:1. McLean study: quasi-psychotic thought, self-mutilation and help-seeking suicide efforts decline fastest; chronic dysphoria/anger/emptiness are the most stable symptoms. 40% remit by 2 years, 88% no longer meet criteria by 10 years.

blocks.title: Bipolar Disorder vs Borderline PD — Differentiating Features

blocks.text: **NICE**: pharmacological treatment is not recommended for personality disorder features themselves, only for comorbid illness (e.g. depression, **OCD**). Suggested symptom-targeted off-label use: antipsychotics for cognitive/perceptual symptoms, SSRIs for affective dysregulation, mood stabilisers/SSRIs for impulsive-behavioural dyscontrol.

sections.title: 15. Sleep Disorders (question-bank only — not covered in the SPMM book notes)

blocks.text: Restless legs syndrome core criteria (mnemonic **URGED**): Urge to move the legs; Rest worsens it; Getting up/moving improves it; Evening/night worsens it; Disorders mimicking **RLS** must be excluded. Supportive criteria include periodic limb movements of sleep, first-degree relatives with **RLS**, and dopaminergic treatment response.

blocks.text: First-line **RLS** treatment: α2δ calcium-channel ligands (**gabapentin**, **pregabalin**) or dopamine agonists (**pramipexole**, **ropinirole**, **rotigotine**); benzodiazepines were used before dopamine agonists became available.

blocks.text: **REM** sleep behaviour disorder: normal **REM** muscle atonia is lost, so dreams are physically acted out; associated lesions are in the brainstem.

blocks.text: Sleep terrors: abrupt panicked awakening with autonomic arousal, no recall, unresponsive during the episode — a disturbance of slow-wave (deep **NREM**) sleep, classified as a **NREM**-related parasomnia alongside sleepwalking.

blocks.text: Snoring has the highest sensitivity (but is nonspecific) for obstructive sleep apnoea among typical symptoms (snoring, nocturnal awakening, nocturia, unrefreshing sleep, daytime sleepiness).

Verify depth against current **NICE** guidance on insomnia/**RLS** and the Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines chapter on hypnotics before relying on this section alone.

blocks.text: Serotonin syndrome vs **NMS**: serotonin syndrome classically shows hyperreflexia and clonus (rigidity can mask these); **NMS**-defining features per **DSM-5** are rigidity and pyrexia. Highest serotonin-syndrome risk is an **MAOI** + **SSRI** combination (e.g. **phenelzine** + **escitalopram**).

blocks.mnemonic: Serotonin syndrome REFLEXES, NMS is RIGID
expansion: Serotonin syndrome: hyperREFLEXia and clonus (onset fast, hours)

blocks.text: Highest serotonin-syndrome risk pairing tested: an **MAOI** (**phenelzine**) plus an **SSRI** (**escitalopram**) in an older adult — combination risk is emphasised over single-drug risk.

blocks.text: Serotonin syndrome's most characteristic sign is hyperreflexia/clonus, which rigidity can mask — this is the deliberate contrast with **NMS** (rigidity + pyrexia) and is a recurring **EMI**/**SBA** discriminator.

blocks.text: Hyponatraemia risk: both SSRIs (especially **citalopram**) and anticonvulsants (especially **carbamazepine**/**oxcarbazepine**) are implicated; reported incidence varies 0.06–40% depending on definition used.

Serum sodium/hyponatraemia risk is most associated with **carbamazepine** among mood stabilisers in one framing and **citalopram** among SSRIs in another — both drugs are independently tested as "most likely to cause hyponatraemia" depending on the option list given, so read the options carefully rather than pattern-matching to one drug.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Adult Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Prolactin elevation is greatest with **risperidone**, **paliperidone**, **amisulpride** and **haloperidol**, and lowest with drugs like **aripiprazole**/**olanzapine**/**quetiapine** (per the Maudsley switching table, **aripiprazole**/**olanzapine**/**quetiapine** are "relatively safe", avoid **amisulpride**).

**CYP2D6** substrates among antidepressants include **clomipramine**, **fluoxetine**, **paroxetine** and **venlafaxine**; **reboxetine** is metabolised via **CYP3A4** instead, making it comparatively unaffected by **CYP2D6** variation.
